speaker: Horace He
title: Horace He: Building Machine Learning Systems for a Trillion Trillion Floating Point Operations
question: In high-performance ML systems, why do engineers often avoid relying on automatic compiler optimizations?
guest: In practice, a lot of times people do not use compilers for high-performance ML, and the reason comes down to how compiler optimizations actually behave. Imagine a library with three features: it does not always work, it has no documentation on when it will work except by reading its source code, and upgrading it can completely change which code works with no backwards compatibility. If 'work' means hitting your desired performance and applying the desired optimization, that largely describes compiler optimizations. As the ISPC article famously put it, auto-vectorization is not a programming model. As long as an automatic optimization can silently fail—and it will—any programmer who actually cares about generated performance has to deeply understand the compiler's internals. When it fails to optimize code you need optimized, you have to poke the compiler or twist your program until it triggers again, which is a horrible way to program. With a proper programming model, the optimization is guaranteed as part of the contract, so you can rely on it without understanding the compiler's implementation.

points.core: Automatic compiler optimizations silently fail to trigger without clear specification rules.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Engineers avoid relying on automatic compiler optimizations mainly because those optimizations are unpredictable and fragile, and the performance stakes are too high to leave to chance.

General-purpose compilers must be conservative: they can only transform code when they can prove it is safe, and things like possible pointer aliasing, strict floating-point semantics, or unknown loop bounds often silently block vectorization. A small, innocent code change or a compiler upgrade can cause an optimization to stop firing, producing a large slowdown with no warning. Compiler heuristics and cost models also lack domain knowledge. They don't know tensor shapes, sparsity, data layouts, cache behavior for a specific workload, or that a loop nest is actually a matrix multiplication best served by a carefully tuned, blocked, architecture-specific kernel.

So engineers make performance explicit: hand-written SIMD intrinsics or assembly, tuned libraries like BLAS, cuDNN, and oneDNN, hand-crafted GPU kernels, and domain-specific compilers such as TVM, Halide, XLA, or MLIR, where scheduling, fusion, and memory layout decisions are controlled directly. This gives guaranteed, reproducible performance, and often far better results than auto-vectorization, at the cost of more engineering effort and less portability.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Engineers in high-performance machine learning often bypass automatic compiler optimizations because general-purpose heuristics struggle to saturate rapidly evolving accelerator hardware and can fail unpredictably. Modern GPUs and TPUs rely on intricate features—such as asynchronous memory transfers, warp specialization, tensor cores, and small, multi-tiered SRAM hierarchies—where reaching roofline performance demands exact control over tiling, memory layouts, and register pressure. Minor changes in tensor shapes or dynamic control flow frequently trigger compiler "performance cliffs," where broken operator fusion or register spilling degrades throughput catastrophically.

Furthermore, breakthrough optimizations like FlashAttention require co-designing mathematical reformulations alongside hardware-aware memory scheduling, crossing floating-point associativity boundaries that compilers conservatively avoid or cannot discover within tractable search spaces. Opaque compilation pipelines also introduce long autotuning times and make diagnosing out-of-memory errors, distributed communication overlap, or numerical drift notoriously difficult. Consequently, when compute utilization directly dictates massive infrastructure costs, engineers favor explicit kernel programming in CUDA, Triton, or Pallas to guarantee predictable, near-optimal execution.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Engineers often avoid relying on automatic compiler optimizations because those optimizations are generic, fragile and hard to predict, and the top performance on ML hardware depends on decisions compilers often get wrong. A compiler like XLA, TorchInductor or plain nvcc uses heuristics tuned for typical code. It may miss the best tiling, memory layout or operator fusion for a specific tensor shape. It may fail to use specialized units such as Tensor Cores or TMA, or it may waste on-chip memory and registers. Peak throughput usually depends on details compilers can't see well: data movement between HBM, shared memory and registers, overlapping communication with computation, and the exact instruction order.

Results also vary. A small code change, a new compiler version or a different input shape can silently disable a fusion or vectorization and cause large slowdowns. That makes performance hard to debug and reproduce. So teams write hand-tuned kernels (FlashAttention is a well-known example), use explicit tools like Triton or CUTLASS, or pin and check the compiler's output. They still use compilers for the common cases, but they control the hot paths that dominate cost by hand.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: In high-performance ML systems, engineers often avoid relying solely on automatic compiler optimizations because compilers struggle with predictability, hardware specificity, and algorithmic co-design. Modern accelerators expose intricate features—like tensor cores, asynchronous memory transfers, shared memory layouts, and tight register budgets—that general-purpose compiler heuristics lag behind in exploiting. Even when compilers perform well, their optimizations are brittle: minor changes in model code, tensor shapes, or compiler versions can silently break operator fusion or memory planning, causing hard-to-diagnose performance regressions. Moreover, the largest speedups often require mathematically restructuring an algorithm to fit the memory hierarchy, such as FlashAttention’s online softmax tiling, which semantics-preserving compiler passes cannot easily invent. Finally, production workloads like LLM serving involve dynamic shapes and control flow that trigger costly recompilations or conservative fallbacks. At massive scale, where small utilization gaps translate into huge compute costs, engineers favor explicit, hand-tuned kernels on critical paths.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Engineers often use compiler optimizations as a baseline, then tune the operations that dominate runtime. The fastest implementation depends on details such as tensor shapes, memory layout, and the target accelerator. A compiler’s cost model can misjudge those trade-offs. For example, fusing two operations can save a trip to GPU memory, but it can also increase register pressure enough to slow the kernel down.

For critical operations, engineers benchmark implementations on the hardware and inputs they actually serve. They may choose a tuned library or write a specialized kernel when measurements show a meaningful gain.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Engineers use compiler optimizations extensively, but they often take direct control of performance-critical code because the fastest implementation depends on details the compiler may not know, such as which tensor shapes are common at runtime. Even when it has that information, the compiler relies on heuristics to choose among many valid implementations, and its choice can perform differently across chips.

For example, two operations can each compile to efficient GPU code while still wasting time writing an intermediate tensor to memory and reading it back. Fusing them into one kernel can eliminate that round trip, but fusion can also increase register pressure and slow the kernel down. Engineers benchmark those choices on the target hardware and use tuned libraries or custom kernels where measurements show a meaningful gain.
